reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .373 xwOBA and .504 xSLG are elite marks, and the 13.3% barrel rate explains why he gets there with regularity rather than in bursts. The catch is the 33.9% chase rate, which keeps a ceiling on the contact floor and is probably why the xBA sits at .262 while the slug numbers look like a different player entirely. If the plate discipline never tightens, you get a guy carrying some of the best contact quality in baseball alongside a 26.1% strikeout rate that bleeds at-bats, and the projection absorbs that tension: 44 home runs and 39 stolen bases at .279, with an 11.5% walk rate doing real work to hold the OBP at .371. At 24 with 29.5 ft/s sprint speed, the floor alone looks like a borderline star, and the ceiling depends entirely on whether that chase rate stays a soft spot or hardens into a genuine vulnerability.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .480 with a 13.0% barrel rate, and those two numbers together explain why the projection lands at 34 home runs despite an average exit velocity that grades only in the 68th percentile — he doesn't need to hit everything hard, just the ones that count. The xwOBA of .351 and projected .812 OPS confirm a legitimate middle-of-the-order bat, not a product of a friendly park or a soft schedule. At 22, the whole profile hinges on whether his contact quality holds against pitchers who will hunt his 26.9% whiff rate with sharper breaking stuff. If it does, he's a 30-plus-homer everyday corner bat; if it doesn't, the power still plays but the average slides toward something that turns him from a lineup centerpiece into a good bench option.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The contact metrics against him as a pitcher tell the story cleanly: a 2.73 xERA, 3.8% barrel rate allowed, and 87.4 mph average exit velocity surrendered, all sitting in the top quarter of the league or better. As a hitter, the .399 xwOBA and 15.8% barrel rate are what you'd expect from a man whose 51.5% hard-hit rate is genuinely elite, and a 13.4% walk rate keeps the on-base floor high even when his 31.5% whiff rate bleeds into the strikeout column. The projection puts him at .277/.380/.524 with 32 home runs across 627 PA, which probably undersells the ceiling if he logs a full two-way workload, and the floor here is not a talent question but a health and usage one: how many innings does Dodger management actually hand him. There is no version of this Statcast profile that reads as ordinary.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.

His 50.5% hard-hit rate and 92.2 mph average exit velocity aren't soft-contact flukes dressed up in good luck — contact quality at that level sustains itself across a full season. Add 43 projected steals to a .817 OPS and you have a shortstop whose value is already elite, with the Statcast profile suggesting the slash line undersells him.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact quality is almost absurdly good for someone who strikes out 27.2% of the time. De La Cruz's 94.5 mph average exit velocity sits at the 99th percentile, his barrel rate is 16.0%, and the underlying expected numbers (.374 xwOBA, .502 xSLG) are each in the 92nd percentile or better, which is why the projection carries .867 OPS despite a strikeout rate that would sink most hitters. The whole profile hinges on whether he keeps enough contact to let the raw power breathe, and right now a 10.8% walk rate is doing real work to offset the whiffs. If the strikeout rate climbs without a corresponding walk bump, the counting stats erode fast, but at 24, with this kind of raw thump and 28 projected steals layered on top, the floor is still a genuine middle-of-the-order threat.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The power contact profile is legitimate and the walk rate is the problem. Merrill's .488 xSLG ranks in a tier where most hitters carry patient approaches; his 6.3% walk rate and 37.0% chase rate are the friction in that story, suppressing a .266 xBA down to a .246 projection AVG and keeping the OBP at .297. What makes him interesting anyway is that the projection still calls for 27 home runs and 27 stolen bases across 671 plate appearances, with 91.3 mph average exit velo and a 48.1% hard-hit rate behind it. Everything hinges on whether he can cut the chase rate enough to let the contact quality breathe, because if he doesn't, the ceiling is a second-division regular with gaudy counting stats in a big lineup, not a star.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: Wood's contact quality is about as good as it gets: 95.3 mph average exit velocity and a 20.5% barrel rate both sit at the 100th percentile, and a 16.8% walk rate means pitchers can't just work around the damage. The problem living inside this elite profile is a 28.3% strikeout rate that belongs to a replacement-level bat, not a .576 xSLG monster, and whether those two things can coexist at scale is the only question that matters. If the strikeouts stabilize anywhere near where the walk rate and 21.8% chase rate suggest they should, the projection's .912 OPS and 33 home runs are a floor, not a ceiling. If they don't, you still have an unusual producer profile, brutal to put away and brutal when he makes contact, just with enough empty at-bats to keep him from being truly great.

reports.name: Jacob Misiorowski
reports.published_report: A 38.3% strikeout rate at the MLB level is the kind of number that ends arguments. Misiorowski's xERA sits at 2.10, his whiff rate at 37.4%, and the 100.6 mph fastball with 2633 rpm spin explains both: hitters aren't just missing, they're missing badly, and when they do make contact the barrel rate is 3.9%. If the 6.7% walk rate holds anywhere near that mark across a full 178.2 projected innings, you're looking at a genuine ace. The dependency is command: if BB% climbs and he loses the ability to expand the zone after getting ahead, the strikeout-to-walk shape softens and what's left is considerably more ordinary.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: The .403 OBP at 18 years old, across three levels including Double-A, is the whole argument. Willits has walked 95 times against 112 strikeouts in 532 plate appearances across AA & A+ & A, a discipline profile that translates to a 12.8% walk rate in MLB context, well above the league mean. The power is the open question: his .191 ISO across AA & A+ & A softens to a .130 MLB equivalent, below average, which means the everyday-regular ceiling runs through the on-base skill holding and the bat speed developing rather than through present thump. Sixty stolen bases sweeten the floor, but if the power doesn't grow, what's left is a high-OBP, plus-speed table-setter who lands closer to a bench or depth outcome than the top of the lineup.

reports.name: Royce Lewis
reports.published_report: The barrel rate (11.4%, 72nd percentile) and the xSLG (.406) say there's a real hitter buried somewhere in this profile. The problem is contact quality and plate discipline pointing in completely opposite directions: he's barreling the ball at an above-average clip while running a 32.4% whiff rate and a 33.5% chase rate that both sit in the bottom quarter of the league, which is exactly how a .312 xwOBA ends up looking like a disappointment instead of a foundation. If he can't tighten his chase approach, the projection's .232/.297/.396 is probably the ceiling rather than the floor — 16 home runs and 15 stolen bases from a guy who strikes out nearly a quarter of the time with below-average on-base rates gives you a second-division regular at best, a roster puzzle at worst.

report_llm.text: 247 strikeouts projected over 185.5 innings tells you what kind of arm Cleveland has here, but the Statcast profile underneath is running two conversations at once. The swing-and-miss is elite: a 33.5% strikeout rate and 32.5% whiff rate that both sit in the 90s percentile-wise, built on a fastball that touches 97.6 mph. The contact-quality numbers run in exactly the opposite direction, a 47.4% hard-hit rate and 11.6% barrel rate that are essentially worst-in-class, and that gap is the whole tension in the profile. Williams gets hitters to swing and miss at a rate that very few starters match, and when they do make contact, they punish it, which is why the xERA settles at 3.79 despite the strikeout volume. If the walk rate, currently a passable 7.8%, creeps up, the strikeouts stop covering the hard contact and this becomes a back-end innings-eater rather than a mid-rotation anchor.

Owen Murphy has a 3.6 ERA over 117.4 innings, which translates to an 87th-percentile mark in his pitcher pool, and his strikeout-minus-walk rate translates to 12.0% at the MLB level — workable, but a back-end starter needs more margin than that. Tighten the walk rate and you get a back-end starter who earns every start; leave it here and the floor is depth.

reports.name: Druw Jones

At AA in 496 plate appearances, Jones is walking 60 times, a disciplined enough approach to post a .357 OBP, but 145 strikeouts give him a 29% K% that translates to 30.3% at the MLB level, well above where most big-league hitters land. The .265 average rides a .379 BABIP and 36 stolen bases carry most of the value; his .104 ISO at AA translates to .099, a figure that sits well short of the .15 MLB-average ISO. reports.name: Logan Henderson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the argument: 4.6% puts Henderson at the 98th percentile, and when you pair that with a 30.2% strikeout rate, the xERA lands at 2.60, also 97th percentile. That combination, contact suppression through control rather than pure swing-and-miss, is exactly the profile that sustains even when the stuff plays down — his 93.1 mph fastball sits 28th percentile, so the margin lives entirely in the command. If the zone control erodes, there's no velo floor to catch him; a walk rate that drifts into ordinary turns this into a back-end arm in a hurry. But as it stands, the projection's 2.58 ERA over 103.7 innings looks like a faithful translation of what the Statcast profile is already saying.

reports.name: Andrés Muñoz
reports.published_report: Thirty saves projected, a 3.20 xERA, and a 41.0% whiff rate that ranks at the very top of the sport — the Statcast profile here is not subtle. Muñoz misses bats at a rate almost no reliever alive matches, and his 37.5% chase rate confirms hitters aren't just expanding the zone out of confusion; they genuinely can't lay off. The one crack in the profile is a 10.2% walk rate that sits well below average, which is what separates a lights-out closer from an untouchable one and is the reason the projection lands at 3.88 ERA rather than somewhere closer to that 3.20 xERA floor. If he tightens the command, the distinction between "excellent closer" and "elite closer" collapses fast.

reports.name: Jared Jones
reports.published_report: The fastball sits at 98.3 mph and spins at 2541 rpm, and that combination is what makes a 32.6% whiff rate believable across a real MLB sample. The walk rate translates to 11.3%, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB norm, and the .377 OBP across AA & A+ shows he's already getting on base at a rate that makes the legs matter. If the contact holds and the stolen-base volume travels to the upper levels, this is a table-setter who earns a lineup spot through on-base and baserunning, not thump; if the power gap widens rather than closes, the floor is a bench bat whose value lives almost entirely in the running game.

reports.name: Matt McLain
reports.published_report: The Statcast card is a contradiction wrapped in a player. McLain's chase rate sits at 26.4%, his walk rate is 10.3%, and his sprint speed grades out near the top of the league at 28.7 ft/s, genuine tools with real plate discipline behind them. The problem is a 28.1% whiff rate dragging his xBA to .220, which means the pitches he does swing at, he's not consistently squaring up, and a .304 xwOBA confirms the contact quality doesn't catch up on enough of them. The projection, .193/.286/.349 over 514 PA, is what happens when good process runs into a contact problem that hasn't been solved, and 17 projected home runs with 19 stolen bases in a near-.200 average year is a fantasy profile attached to a real defensive asset (91st-percentile OAA) who can't quite hit enough to make it work. If the whiff rate comes down and the 9.5% barrel rate plays to its actual frequency, he's a useful regular; if it doesn't, he's a very fast, very good-fielding second baseman with a .193 average.

reports.name: Luke Stevenson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument, and it's also the ceiling. Stevenson has drawn 98 walks across 474 plate appearances at A+, a BB% that ranks in the 98th percentile of his pool, sitting next to a .405 OBP and 22 home runs that give the profile real shape on paper. But the MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout rate at 32.3%, well past the 22.0% MLB average, and ISO translates to .162, roughly league-average power, not the plus-power the raw A+ line implies. The discipline is loud and likely real at the next level; the one dependency the whole profile rests on is whether that contact rate tightens, and if it doesn't, what's left is a catching prospect with a patient eye and marginal bat-to-ball skills whose ceiling is organizational depth.

reports.name: Dylan O'Rae
reports.published_report: The profile is built entirely on plate discipline and stolen bases, and the power is almost nowhere. Sixty-five walks against 77 strikeouts across 419 AA plate appearances is a real skill set, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his walk rate at 12.0%, nearly half again what a typical big-leaguer draws, but the ISO translates to .098 in that same context while most MLB hitters land around .150, which means the bat has to do everything through contact and speed. Fifty-eight stolen bases at AA will get scouts to the ballpark, but if the gap between his on-base ability and his slugging (.370 at AA, 36th percentile among this pool) doesn't close, he's a bench piece who lives on patience and legs rather than a regular. The ceiling is thin enough that this profile hinges entirely on whether that speed translates and the hit tool holds, and if contact regresses, the .395 OBP at AA becomes the whole argument.

reports.name: Hayden Alvarez
reports.published_report: The 53 stolen bases are the loudest thing in this profile, and they're also the thing that matters most for whether any of this translates. Across A+ & A, Alvarez is hitting .289/.391/.456 with 75 walks against 109 strikeouts in 551 plate appearances, a contact-and-patience line that looks real at this level but softens considerably when you run it through MLB-equivalent context: the walk rate holds up, translating to 10.2% where MLB average sits at 8.5%, but the ISO drops to .115 and the strikeout rate climbs to 25.2%. The speed is the separator, because without plus run value the power floor is thin and the OBP doesn't carry a lineup spot on its own. Either the speed stays elite and he becomes a table-setter who earns a bench role through his legs, or the bat thins out against better velocity and he's organizational depth.

reports.name: Blake Mitchell
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing on this card, and it's also the problem. At A+ in 2026, Blake Mitchell has drawn 113 walks in 511 plate appearances, a 22% clip that sits at the 99th percentile of his pool, and he's added 27 stolen bases and 23 home runs on top of it, a legitimately unusual combination for a catcher at 21. But the .234 average against a .346 BABIP tells you the strikeouts aren't disappearing, and when that contact rate translates to an MLB-equivalent 36.8% K%, what survives the jump is a 15.4% walk rate propped up against average power at .152 ISO. The whole profile hinges on whether the discipline holds as pitchers locate better, because if the strikeouts climb and the walks compress even modestly, the .234 average becomes the story rather than the footnote. If it works, he's a patient, borderline-average offensive catcher who runs; if it doesn't, the bench is the ceiling.

He's fanning 33% of the time at AAA, and that translates to a 31.1% clip against MLB pitching, well past the 22.0% MLB average, with a walk rate that would sit just below league average. The power shows in a .180 ISO at AAA, but the translated .146 ISO lands right at the MLB mean, which means the gap between the raw tool and what survives the level jump isn't wide enough to carry the contact profile. If the strikeout rate doesn't come down, what's left is a bench bat with some right-handed pop and not much else.

reports.name: Isaac Lyon
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing real work here. Across AAA & AA & A+ & A in 2026, the 2.6 BB/9 and 1.1 WHIP translate to a walk figure that lands just below the MLB baseline of 3.2, which is the only reason a strikeout rate this modest stays interesting. His 8.2 K/9 in the minors translates to 7.2 at the big-league level, well short of the 8.6 MLB average, and that gap is the whole profile in miniature: Lyon commands the zone well enough to function, but not well enough to miss bats and get away with it. If the control holds and he gets soft contact, there's a backend piece somewhere in here; if hitters adjust and the walks tick up even slightly, the strikeout rate has no cushion to absorb it.

reports.name: Xavier Rivas
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate translates, the walk rate doesn't. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Rivas has punched out 128 batters in 97.6 innings, and that 11.8 K/9 renders to a 9.4 MLB-equivalent — a tick past what most big-league starters post. The walk rate renders to 5.2 at the MLB level, nearly two full runs above where the average pitcher lands, and that gap is why a K-BB% sitting at the 77th percentile against his pitcher pool still translates to a below-average 12.7% in MLB terms. If the command sharpens enough to close even half that gap, there's a useful reliever here; if it doesn't, the strikeouts alone won't carry a rotation spot and he settles into a depth or short-burst bullpen role.

reports.name: Sebastian Dos Santos
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the lead. Forty-four walks in 255 plate appearances at A-ball, a 17% clip that translates to 11.3% at the MLB level while the MLB average sits at 8.5%, is a disciplined zone approach on an 18-year-old shortstop who isn't supposed to have that skill yet. The .400 OBP is carrying a .246 average, which tells you exactly where the value lives. What's uncertain is the power: a .191 ISO at A looks promising, but the MLB-equivalent lands at .130, below average, and a 27.5% strikeout translation suggests the bat-to-ball side will be tested hard as the level rises. If the walk rate survives the jump and the contact improves even a little, he becomes a low-end regular; if the strikeouts spike and the discipline regresses, what's left is a bench bat with a useful on-base skill.

reports.name: Aroon Escobar
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the one thing working for him, and it's not enough. At AA in 558 plate appearances, Aroon Escobar has posted a 16 K% that translates to 19.6% against big-league pitching, comfortably under the MLB baseline of 22.0%, and his 12 BB% gets him to a translated 10.0% walk rate, better than most hitters see at that level. The discipline package is genuine. What isn't is the bat: a .225/.330/.328 slash at AA with a .103 ISO, and when that ISO translates to .097 against MLB arms, you're looking at a hitter who doesn't hit the ball hard enough to carry the profile even with clean plate appearances. The ceiling here is whether the power develops enough to close the gap, and if it doesn't, the walk rate and 26 stolen bases in 558 AA plate appearances buy him a bench spot, nothing more.

reports.name: Boston Smith
reports.published_report: The .424 OBP and 31 home runs across AA & A+ & A would be a lead story for almost any prospect — except the 140 strikeouts are the ceiling tax. He draws walks at a rate that translates to 14.5% in MLB context, well above what the average big-leaguer posts, and the power translates to a .196 ISO, clear of the .150 MLB mean. The problem is that 29 K% in the minors becomes 31.4% against big-league arms, and for a catcher that kind of contact erosion tends to eat the defensive slack teams are willing to grant. If the strikeout rate firms up even a little, there's a genuine offensive profile here; if it doesn't, what's left is a walk-heavy catcher with fringe contact, which is a bench job at best.

Across A+ & A, Chirinos has posted a 3.3 BB/9 and a 3.4 ERA over 114 innings, which grades well inside his pitcher pool, but his 9.9 K/9 translates to roughly 7.5 at the MLB level, a tick below what MLB starters typically need to stick. A 17% K-BB% sounds workable until the translation cuts it to 11.0%, well short of the 13.5% MLB average. The floor and ceiling land in the same place: a depth arm whose viability depends entirely on whether the strikeout rate grows as the competition does, and if it doesn't, the command advantage alone won't hold a big-league job.

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the argument here. At A-ball, Genao has issued 33 walks across 108 innings, which translates to a 90th-percentile BB/9 among peers — and when the command is that clean at 20, the rest of the profile earns a second look. The strikeout rate is honest rather than exciting: 116 punchouts in those same 108 innings at A looks fine, but it translates to 7.1 per nine against big-league hitters, well short of the MLB average. reports.name: Luke Dickerson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that makes the rest of it complicated. Across A+ & A, Luke Dickerson has drawn 106 walks against 159 strikeouts in 527 plate appearances, a 20% walk rate that sits at the 97th percentile of his peer pool, paired with a .218 average and a .312 BABIP that suggests he isn't running on luck to get there. The MLB-equivalent translation puts his walk rate at 13.8%, well above the 8.5% major-league figure, but the strikeout rate translates to 35% where the big-league number is 22%, and the ISO comes through at .118, below what a lineup regular needs to carry a spot on his own. If the contact rate doesn't improve as he climbs, what's left is a patient hitter without enough damage attached to the discipline, and the floor stays firmly in organizational depth.
